rounds.evidence_text: On a night when the roar of go-karts was silenced by a nefarious deed, Detective Winston finds himself investigating the peculiar murder of Gary, slain by a rarely-seen sai with two unlikely suspects: Frederick and Jerome.
Detective Winston flicked through the reports once again.
The guy is a dock worker, moved shipping containers around all day.
It was a harmless hobby, but it didn't sit right.

"The dock's a rough place, Winston," said Officer Daniels, a baby-faced officer with a knack of not following orders, "You can't be weak and thrive there."

"I bet Frederick's co-workers would tell you about his strength and dexterity.
Cargo isn't a walk in the park," Winston said, taking in Daniels' recommendation.
Strength and dexterity...
it reminded him of something.
The weapon, a sai, was found in Frederick's collection.
Winston rubbed his brow lightly and continued turning the pages.
Frederick was a devotee of warfare artifacts.
From ancient katana to modern assault rifles, Frederick had them all.
"Frederick goes for racing during his free time," the report read.
In fact, suspicious activity at the go-kart track was often reported around Frederick's usual racing time.
Winston remembered Frederick's racing schedule: every Thursday at six, without fail.
On the day Gary was killed, Frederick and Gary were both at the go-kart track.
Gary, a joker at heart, was seen messing around with Frederick's go-kart, the very same one that Frederick had previously confronted others about.
Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair.
Daniels had a defensive glance in his eye.
"But he's just an enthusiast!
And skilled, I heard," Daniels defended, almost pleadingly.
Winston only nodded, his mind already spinning with strategies and weak alibis.
"He's also a dockworker, known for his strength and dexterity, able to handle heavy cargo safely." He paused.

"Isn't a sai a pretty lightweight weapon?"

"Yes sir." Daniels stuttered out, not daring to look Winston in the eye.
"Frederick..." he swallowed.

"Frederick might have the skill to wield a sai."

Winston continued reviewing the reports and evidence, his mind far from eased, his heart heavy with the task at hand.
The dockworker.
The go-kart track.
The sai.
The confrontations over the go-kart.
The timelines adding up just so...
Suspicions were nothing until proven in the court of law.
But still, it was a start.
Time to pay Frederick a visit.
Clouds hovered above the go-kart track as Winston surveyed the murder scene.
The sight of Gary's lifeless body had been replaced by yellow police tape, but the stain of what had occurred remained imprinted in Winston's mind.
Indisputably, Gary was the current go-kart champion of their small town.
A title that endowed him a sense of invincibility and an obstacle for Jerome, the runner up more times than Jerome cared to admit.
Winston pulled the collar of his coat up, glancing around the track at the groups of people, all huddled up and whispering.
Among the crowd, his eyes locked onto a man standing alone, pressing binoculars to his eyes.

rounds.evidence_text: When Wendy's life brutally ended under the sharp end of a pickaxe at the local roller rink, it was up to the shrewd Detective Winston to untangle the web spun around two prime suspects, Marianne and Sidney.

It projected grainy CCTV footage of his suspect - Marianne.
She was there at the roller rink, on the night poor Wendy met her end.
Not only was Marianne there - she was seen shouting at Wendy, their voices escalating until they pierced the rhythmic hum of the skating wheels.
The timestamp of the argument, and subsequent footage of Marianne lingering, suggested she was there for quite some time after her dispute with Wendy.
He thumbed through a thin folder tucked beneath a closing pizza box resting on his cluttered desk.
Marianne had a criminal record, it revealed a past fraught with moments of explosion, of violence - including an assault arrest five years prior.
The Marianne on the screen, the Marianne in these documents had been caught in the wrong before.
Winston began to feel a creeping uneasiness as he parsed this correlation.
Several pictures tumbled from the folder as Winston shuffled its contents.
The pictures were snapshots of Marianne: caught in the midst of her day-to-day, widely recognized by the community - not just for her nature but for her frequent use of an old pickaxe.
It came as no surprise since she had spent several years working in the mines before her marriage.
She was seen using her pickaxe for numerous tasks such as chopping firewood or loosening soil in her garden.
"Did you see what she was doing last week?" a seasoned woman down the road had mentioned as she was reversing her car out of the driveway.
Marianne was seen cleaning her well-worn mining equipment that she'd kept stored in an easily accessible tool-shed next to her house in clear sight.
It seemed she wasn't shy about flaunting her past or the tools she used while in the mines.
Commotion at the precinct broke Winston from his thoughts.
The crime-scene analyst reported the murder took place in some remote corner of the roller rink.
Despite the public dispute that took place earlier between Wendy and Marianne, this location seemed isolated, uncanny for such a busy locale.
The analyst's words seemed to chisel further into Winston's thoughts as he returned to the grainy images.
Her mining equipment was never far from reach, and Marian's cacophony on the night of Wendy's murder was caught on tape.
Pieces started falling into place; too many strings tethered Marianne to the night Wendy was murdered.
With a sigh, Winston allowed himself a quiet moment.
Then, taking a deep breath, he began his descent into the intricacies of the case before him.
Winston stood at the entrance of the roller rink, eyes scanning the room.
The images from the crime scene report replayed in his memory.
Poor Wendy had breathed her last in what was supposed to be a place filled with the rejuvenating sounds of retro music and flashing lights.
Sidney, who was a geologist, had been seen with Wendy at the roller rink multiple times.
According to the staff, Sidney was even a regular here.
It was a curious detail but not unusual, people had hobbies apart from their professions.
Sidney's passion besides analyzing layers of earth was rollerblading.
He frequently carried his tools, including his pickaxe, from his daytime geological survey sites directly to the roller rink in the evenings.
Checking his notes from the previous conversation with Sidney, his eyebrows knitted slightly as he remembered the desperation he sensed from Sidney.
It revolved around Wendy, who apparently knew something he coveted as a secret.
She had been sharing this secret with her friends and it seemed it held the power to publicly humiliate Sidney if it ever came to light.
Sidney, for his part, vehemently denied any secret of such scale.
Winston gestured for the barista to come over.
The young man with a skater haircut glanced at Winston's badge before he ordered a black coffee with no sugar.

While waiting for his order, he asked, “Did you notice Sidney here during the time of the incident?”

The barista nodded, nervously biting his lower lip.

In fact, during their investigation, the police found no documented ties of Clara with the deceased individuals, either.
Over black coffee and stale bread in a nearby diner, Detective Winston conversed with Clarence.
"So you’re a truck driver?
Tough gig, I imagine," Winston started the conversation the way he always did, meandering towards his point while observing reactions.
"You bet.
I've been doing this job for a while now, driving all sorts of routes.
Comes with its own set of challenges, like finding a decent mechanic on the go.
I had to learn repairing my truck on my own.
Hence, the toolbox you see me lugging around," Clarence responded.

Detective Winston veered the discussion towards Vanessa, "And what brings you around the synagogue frequently?"

"Well, work mostly.
But it’s no secret - Vanessa, she and me...
We used to be together.
She'd often be at the synagogue.
Despite how things ended with us, my old habits never really changed," Clarence replied with a forlorn sigh.
As Winston remembered Vanessa's face and Clarence's haggard expression, sleep felt like a distant luxury.
Skimming through the raw facts in his notebook, this was no game of conjectures, the hard evidence was yet to fit in the puzzle.
And with that last thought, he closed the notebook shut for the night.
Detective Winston stood, perched in the corner of the local hardware store.
He watched from behind a pyramid of paint cans, peering at Ivy as she demonstrated a new set of screwdrivers to a customer.
Overalls clad, she seemed like an everyday, hard-working woman.
She completed the sale and moved on to help the next customer, carrying another set of similar tools to the customer who was looking for a specific size.
It was clear that she moved deftly and knew her products well.
It troubled Winston how an ordinary day selling hardware could be turned on its head so rapidly, by a single piece of information.
Winston decided to make his move.
He stepped out from his hiding place, adjusting the collar of his trench coat to protect from the sudden gust of wind that swept through the open door.
“Hello, Ivy,” he said, his gaze piercing through her.
Dropping her head down, the terror and desperation in Ivy’s eyes were evident.

Caught in a blackmail situation over deep secrets that Vanessa had threatened to reveal, secrets that could ruin her reputation, it was serving harsh punishments on her livelihood in the form of lost customers.
She feared her secrets would come out any day now.
It was this fear that had greeted Winston when Ivy arrived at the synagogue that morning, noticeably before Vanessa's life was tragically ended there.
Refusing to meet his gaze, she nodded, inviting him to continue.
